case_prompt:
A 24-year-old Southeast Asian woman presented with a 2-month history of pruritic blisters and bullae initially on her hands that gradually involved her face and trunk. She also reported weight loss, myalgia, fatigue, intermittent fever, self-limiting epistaxis, and hair loss. She denied dyspnea, hematuria, decreased urine output, muscle weakness, joint pain, or new medications.

On examination, temperature and respiratory rate were normal; pulse was 112 beats per minute; blood pressure was 80/60 mmHg; oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Findings included non-cicatricial hair loss, pallor, a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, and discoid lesions on the ears. Numerous tense, clear vesicles and bullae on an erythematous base involved her face, nape of neck, trunk, and hands. Superficial erosions were noted on the buccal mucosa, hard palate, and lips. The Nikolsky sign and bulla spread sign were positive; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Initial laboratory studies revealed a white-cell count of 2600/mm³, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, aspartate aminotransferase 194 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 53 U/L, albumin 2.9 g/L, active urinary sediments with white cells and albumin, and proteinuria of 0.42 g/24 h. Peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia with pencil and teardrop cells. Antinuclear antibody testing was positive; erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 18 mm/h; C-reactive protein was 1.8 mg/L (normal 0–4.8); and complement levels were slightly decreased.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Bullous systemic lupus erythematosus was considered given underlying SLE manifestations and widespread tense vesicles and bullae — “Bullous systemic lupus erythematosus (BSLE) is a blistering disease characterized by tense subepidermal fluid‐filled vesicles and bullae. The common sites of involvement include the face, trunk, neck, extensor surfaces of upper limbs, and oral mucosa.” 2. Dermatitis herpetiformis was considered because of pruritic vesicles but is typically intensely pruritic on extensor surfaces rather than sun‐exposed skin — “Predilection to extensor surfaces, elbows, knees, and buttocks; intensely pruritic.” 3. Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita was considered due to subepidermal blistering but usually occurs without SLE and heals with scarring — “Absence of SLE; heal with scarring and milia formation.” 4. Bullous pemphigoid was considered given tense bullae but often presents with eosinophil‐rich infiltrates and a prodrome of pruritus without mucosal involvement — “Prodrome of moderate to severe pruritus +/− urticarial, papular lesions; responsive to corticosteroids.” 5. Linear IgA bullous dermatosis was considered as it can mimic other bullous diseases but shows linear IgA deposition on split skin — “Linear deposition of IgA on the epidermal side of split skin. Resembles dermatitis herpetiformis.”

selection.screen_reason: Tense bullae with malar and discoid rash, alopecia, cytopenias, nephritis and positive ANA point to bullous SLE.
selection.second_look_note: Pruritic blisters with fever, weight loss and hair loss, tense bullae with malar and discoid rash, cytopenias, active urine sediment and positive ANA point to bullous SLE.
